A specific idea tied to its subject: Leonardo's notebooks (Vitruvian Man, flying machines, mirror-script pages, the Mona Lisa) are layered with ink-drawn figures. Only this show could have this opening.
Dense, layered frames: hand-inked line work over painted skies, paper grain, ink spatter and vellum texture, with real depth between the layers.
Deliberate palette of bruised violet, sepia and bone, with tone shifting from frame to frame instead of a single accent colour.

Composition changes in every frame: a centred figure, an architectural elevation with perspective lines, an extreme close-up of a pen nib, a horizon split with a tiny rider, a face looking upward framed by a circle, a diagonal figure with a crossbow. This shows choreography, not a repeated template.
Credits are set in small caps in a classical serif that fits the period. They sit in the negative space of each composition rather than at a fixed position.
gaps: The typography is fitting but conservative. The credits never interact with the ink, the geometry or the mirror script, so the type has less of an idea than the image does.
Some frames lean on familiar 'grunge illustration' textures and a purple grade that dates the piece. A more restrained or surprising grade would set it apart.
The central idea (the da Vinci sketchbook come to life) is apt but expected. There is no single image as surprising or emotionally charged as D's jewelled bird crossing New York.

tells: A clear narrative device: a jewelled, articulated bird and its particle trail carry the viewer through connected worlds (a clock face, an overhead street with a yellow cab, a ballet stage, brownstone windows, a dinner table, a painted desert mesa).
Real cinematic light: practical bokeh, candle and window glow, volumetric stage beams, specular sparkle on the jewelled metal. Materials read as precious metal, brick, porcelain and paint.

Strong variety in camera and scale (an overhead plan, a close-up through a clock, a wide stage, a balcony view), and the recurring sparkle trail links the shots, which suggests choreographed transitions.
A bold shift in style to a painterly desert in the final frame shows confidence and an element of surprise.
No type is visible. Its absence serves a brand film that relies on image alone.
gaps: The vocabulary is luxury-holiday-campaign familiar: a magical sparkle trail, a New York taxi, a ballerina. The idea is executed superbly but is not new.
No typographic idea is visible. A considered end-frame or title integrated with the bird's trail would make it complete as a piece of motion design.
The tonal range jumps between photoreal CG and painted illustration without visible logic in the sampled frames. The bridge needs to be clearer to read as one authored world.

Objects are chosen with no visible connecting idea, and the logic in the details is off (a chess board with nonsensical pieces, a plug merging into a glowing porthole). This is typical of image-generator output.

gaps: There is no concept connecting the objects. It needs an idea, a narrative or a transformation logic that would make these specific things belong in one film.
Every frame is a centred hero object on a seamless backdrop. It needs compositional variety, scale contrast, environment and depth.
There is no evidence of motion design. It needs transitions, morphs or camera choreography that link one object to the next, as A and D do.

defects: 100% crop: the wall/floor horizon line shows hard stair-step aliasing; it reads as a raw real-time render edge, not a resolved one
Plant foliage has cutout or alpha-card edges with hard dark fringes and no soft self-shadowing, so the leaves look like pasted textures against the softly lit wall
Contact shadows are weak or missing: pots seem to float on the table (frame 2 close-up, frame 3 urn), and the large blurry wall shadows aren't anchored to any object
The white pot carries an odd melted-looking tag or spout attachment that reads as a modelling artefact at close-up
Floor type ('Not yet.', 'Sunday.', 'A splash.') is a generic heavy sans with soft, blurry perspective rendering, and the 'loam' wordmark is cropped at the frame edge mid-move
Pairs show almost no change 1/6 s apart in every row: the shots are slow, uneased camera drifts over static sets, which counts as dead air
There is a 5.0 s hold, and 3/14 seconds look the same as the previous second; the end tag sits static for about 4 s with only a light change
End card: 'Out now.' is set in a second, smaller green type treatment that clashes with the grey floor-projected system
gaps: Motion: no real choreography. Nothing grows, gets watered, sways or reacts, and the 'splash' moment shows no splash. The idea (the plant's answer written on the floor) needs a physical event in each shot: soil darkening, leaves lifting, a shadow sweeping across as time passes. Instead it's a camera dolly over still life. Top studios would also use the window-light shadow sweep as the transition between shots rather than hard cuts.

Sound: the spectrogram shows one repeated pluck or percussion loop with a flat, static wideband noise bed (5.6–7.6 s) and a dropout to silence (~9–10 s). That's the only dynamic gesture, and it isn't clearly tied to a cut or to the reveal. There's no foley (water, soil, ceramic) and no sound design selling the material world, and nothing visible lands on the transients.

Finish: real-time-engine quality, with an aliased horizon, cutout foliage, floating pots and soft, low-contrast floor type. The wall texture and light falloff are pleasant, but the render needs AA, proper contact occlusion, leaf subsurface and crisper projected type to reach studio level. The energy curve is also flat, with no build to a peak before the logo.
